questions.stem: The BHAKTI MOVEMENT in medieval India emphasised:

options.option_text: Personal DEVOTION (bhakti) to a single God; rejection of elaborate ritual + caste distinctions; use of REGIONAL LANGUAGES

questions.explanation: BHAKTI MOVEMENT — religious reform movement in India that emphasised DEVOTION (bhakti) to a personal God as the path to salvation, over Vedic ritualism + priestly intermediaries. ORIGINS: South India 7th-12th c. with the ALVARS (Vaishnavite saints devoted to Vishnu, 12 of them) + NAYANARS (Shaivite saints devoted to Shiva, 63 of them) — composed hymns in TAMIL. KEY FEATURES: (1) Direct devotion to God, no need for Brahmin intermediary; (2) rejection of caste discrimination — saints came from low + high castes alike; (3) use of REGIONAL languages (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Marathi, Hindi, Bengali, Punjabi) instead of Sanskrit; (4) composed DEVOTIONAL POETRY accessible to masses; (5) emphasis on unity of God (monotheism or monism). SPREAD TO NORTH INDIA — from 13th-17th c. via saints like Ramananda, Kabir, Nanak, Chaitanya, Meerabai, Tulsidas, Surdas. DIVIDED into SAGUNA (God with form — e.g. Rama, Krishna devotion: Tulsidas, Surdas, Meera) + NIRGUNA (God without form — e.g., Kabir, Nanak). HISTORICAL SIGNIFICANCE: promoted HINDU-MUSLIM synthesis, democratised religion, enriched regional literature, laid foundation for modern Indian vernaculars. CONTEMPORARY SUFI movement in Islam had parallel themes.

questions.stem: KABIR (c. 1440-1518) was the disciple of which teacher, and he rejected the distinctions of both Hinduism + Islam?

options.option_text: RAMANANDA — the Vaishnavite saint of Varanasi who opened bhakti to all castes + faiths

questions.explanation: KABIR (c. 1440-1518) — one of the greatest NIRGUNA bhakti saints of N India. BIRTH: said to be born to a Brahmin widow, abandoned + raised by a MUSLIM WEAVER family in Varanasi (hence Kabir — an Arabic name meaning 'the great'). DISCIPLE OF RAMANANDA — the 14th-c. Vaishnavite saint based in Varanasi, himself a disciple-tradition successor of Ramanuja. Ramananda broke caste barriers by teaching bhakti to ALL — his 12 named disciples included Kabir (weaver-Muslim), Ravidas (chamar), Sena (barber), Dhanna (Jat peasant), Pipa (Rajput king), Padmavati (woman), etc. KABIR'S TEACHINGS: (1) ONE formless God (Nirguna); (2) Rejected idolatry, pilgrimage, rituals of BOTH Hindus + Muslims; (3) Criticised caste distinctions (some of the sharpest social critiques in Indian literature — 'If God is in a mosque, whose is the world outside?'); (4) Advocated unity of all religions; (5) used the metaphor of God as the unseen weaver. WORKS: DOHAS (couplets) + SAKHIS; compiled in BIJAK (by his Kabirpanthi followers); 500+ of his verses in the GURU GRANTH SAHIB. DEATH MYTH: died at MAGHAR (near Gorakhpur, UP) — deliberately to reject the superstition that death at Varanasi guarantees moksha; when his followers quarrelled over burial (Muslim) vs cremation (Hindu), his body was said to turn into flowers — divided between the two. Kabirpanthis remain active today.

questions.stem: GURU NANAK DEV (1469-1539), founder of Sikhism, was born in:

options.option_text: TALWANDI (now NANKANA SAHIB, in Pakistan's Punjab)

questions.explanation: GURU NANAK DEV JI (1469-1539) — founder of SIKHISM, first of the TEN SIKH GURUS. BIRTH: 15 April 1469, TALWANDI village, now called NANKANA SAHIB in honour of him, in Punjab, Pakistan (~75 km from Lahore). BIRTH ANNIVERSARY ('Gurpurab') celebrated on full moon of Kartik (Nov). TEACHINGS: (1) IK ONKAR — 'One Supreme God'; (2) rejected caste, ritualism, blind faith; (3) equality of men + women; (4) three pillars — NAAM JAPO (meditate on God's name), KIRAT KARO (honest work), VAND CHAKKO (share with others); (5) LANGAR (community kitchen) — free meal for all, regardless of caste/religion. UDASIS: undertook FOUR great travels (udasis) across S Asia, W Asia, Tibet — met Muslim Sufis + Hindu yogis. COMPANION: his Muslim minstrel BHAI MARDANA accompanied him. FOUNDED KARTARPUR: last years at Kartarpur (now in Pak Punjab, visible from Dera Baba Nanak in India — Kartarpur Corridor opened Nov 2019 for pilgrims). SUCCESSOR: named BHAI LEHNA as his successor + renamed him Guru Angad (2nd Sikh Guru). COMPOSITIONS: 974 hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib (JAPJI SAHIB being the most famous — recited daily by Sikhs). Guru Nanak is revered by Hindus, Sikhs, + many Muslims; called 'BABA NANAK' affectionately.

questions.stem: MEERABAI, the Rajput princess-poet devoted to Krishna, belonged to which royal house?

options.option_text: MARRIED into MEWAR (Sisodia) house of CHITTOR but was a princess of MERTA (Rathore) branch in Marwar — a grand-daughter of Rao Duda

questions.explanation: MEERABAI (c. 1498-1547) — greatest WOMAN bhakti saint-poet. BIRTH: MERTA (Rajasthan) in the Rathore clan; grand-daughter of Rao Duda of Merta. MARRIAGE: at ~18 to BHOJRAJ, crown prince of Mewar (Chittor, Sisodia Rajputs); son of RANA SANGA. Bhojraj died young (~1521 from war wounds). WIDOWHOOD: Meera refused to commit Sati, refused to worship family deity Durga (her loyalty was to Krishna alone); faced persecution from in-laws — Rana VIKRAMADITYA (her brother-in-law) tried to poison her (legend: the poison turned to nectar) + sent a serpent in a basket (turned into Krishna's garland). She left Chittor + wandered as a wandering devotee. DEATH: ~1547 at DWARKA (Gujarat), said to merge into the image of Krishna at Dwarkadhish temple. DEVOTION: to KRISHNA, whom she called 'GIRDHAR NAGAR' / 'Giridhar Gopal' — envisioning herself as his eternal wife. BHAJANS: composed in Rajasthani + Braj Bhasha; hundreds survive; themes of divine love, rejection of worldly ties, defiance of patriarchy. Famous bhajans: 'Mere to Giridhar Gopal', 'Paayo ji maine Ram Ratan Dhan Paayo'. ICONIC for CHALLENGING Rajput feudal + patriarchal norms; early 'feminist' voice in Indian literature; revered across N India. Shortcut for memorisation: MEERA = Merta-born, Mewar-married, Krishna-devoted.

questions.stem: TULSIDAS (1532-1623) is known for composing the:

options.option_text: RAMCHARITMANAS — retelling of the Rama story in AWADHI (a dialect of Hindi), making it accessible to non-Sanskrit-reading masses

questions.explanation: TULSIDAS (1532-1623) — greatest SAGUNA bhakti poet of North India, devotee of Lord RAMA. MAGNUM OPUS: RAMCHARITMANAS ('The Lake of the Deeds of Rama'), started 1574 at Ayodhya; composed in AWADHI (a dialect of Hindi) — breaking with the Sanskrit norm so that common folk could read + sing it. Still the most-read Hindu religious text in the Hindi belt; basis of Ramleela performances across N India (UNESCO ICH 2005). STRUCTURE: 7 KANDAS (like Valmiki Ramayana) — Bal, Ayodhya, Aranya, Kishkindha, Sundar, Lanka, Uttar. OTHER WORKS: Vinay Patrika, Kavitavali, Hanuman Chalisa (40 verses — most-recited Hindu devotional in India). LIFE: born in Rajapur (Chitrakoot region), UP; guru was Narharidas; lived mostly at Varanasi + Chitrakoot. LEGEND: inspired to retell Ramayana when his wife RATNAVALI chided him for his excessive attachment to her saying 'If you loved Rama as you love me, you'd attain Him' — transformed Tulsidas into a renunciate + poet-saint. CONTRIBUTION: (1) made Rama bhakti central to Hindi-belt Hinduism; (2) literary standard for Awadhi; (3) Hanuman Chalisa — most popular Indian devotional text today; (4) influenced Vaishnava culture + the conception of ideal king (RAMA-RAJYA). Contemporary of Akbar + Abul Fazl.

questions.stem: SHANKARACHARYA (Adi Shankara, 788-820 CE) propounded the philosophy of:

options.option_text: ADVAITA VEDANTA — absolute non-dualism: Brahman is the only reality; the world is Maya (illusion); Atman = Brahman

questions.explanation: ADI SHANKARACHARYA (788-820 CE) — philosopher-saint from KALADI (Kerala); FOUNDER of ADVAITA VEDANTA (pure non-dualism). CORE DOCTRINE: BRAHMAN is the only ultimate reality (sat-chit-ananda — existence-consciousness-bliss); the phenomenal world (jagat) is MAYA (appearance); the individual soul (ATMAN) is IDENTICAL with Brahman ('Aham Brahmasmi', 'Tat Tvam Asi'). Liberation (moksha) = realisation of this identity. ACHIEVEMENT: in a short 32-year life, he: (1) travelled all of India debating scholars (DIG-VIJAYA); (2) wrote commentaries (bhashyas) on 10 Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita, Brahma Sutras (the 'PRASTHANATRAYI'); (3) authored Vivekachudamani, Bhaja Govindam, Saundaryalahari, etc.; (4) established FOUR MATHAS (monastic seats) in India's four corners: Sringeri (South, Karnataka), Dwarka (West, Gujarat), Jyotirmath/Badrinath (North, UK), Puri (East, Odisha); (5) organised DASHANAMI SANNYASA tradition (10 orders of monks); (6) revived + reformulated Hinduism against Buddhist + Jain ascendancy of his time. CHALLENGER: RAMANUJA (1017-1137) later developed VISHISHTADVAITA ('qualified non-dualism') — Brahman is real + the world + souls are His attributes, not illusion. MADHVACHARYA (1238-1317) went further with DVAITA ('dualism') — God, soul, world are distinct. VALLABHA — Shuddhadvaita. NIMBARKA — Dvaitadvaita.

questions.stem: CHAITANYA MAHAPRABHU (1486-1534), who popularised the worship of Krishna through Sankirtan (congregational chanting), was based primarily in:

options.option_text: NABADWIP (Bengal) + PURI (Odisha) — founded the GAUDIYA VAISHNAVISM tradition

questions.explanation: CHAITANYA MAHAPRABHU (1486-1534) / 'Gauranga' — Bengal's greatest bhakti saint; founder of GAUDIYA VAISHNAVISM. BIRTH: NABADWIP / Navadweep, Nadia district, West Bengal (an ancient centre of Sanskrit learning — sometimes called 'Oxford of Bengal'). Initially a scholar; renounced worldly life at 24 after receiving initiation from Ishwara Puri in Gaya. Spent most of his later years in PURI (Odisha) — at the Jagannath temple. TEACHINGS: (1) Most intense devotion to KRISHNA + RADHA as the supreme couple — 'Krishna-prema'; (2) method = SANKIRTAN / Nama-sankirtan — congregational chanting of God's name, esp. the 16-word MAHA-MANTRA 'Hare Krishna Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna Hare Hare, Hare Rama Hare Rama, Rama Rama Hare Hare'; (3) open to ALL, regardless of caste or creed; (4) emotional devotion (bhava bhakti) as supreme means to moksha. SIX GOSWAMIS: his learned disciples — Rupa, Sanatana, Raghunatha Bhatta, Raghunatha Dasa, Gopala Bhatta, Jiva — systematised his theology + rebuilt Vrindavan's Krishna temples. MODERN IMPACT: ISKCON (International Society for Krishna Consciousness, founded 1966 by A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada) directly descends from Gaudiya Vaishnavism — took 'Hare Krishna' movement worldwide. AUROBINDO + TAGORE were both influenced by Chaitanya's Bengal Vaishnav tradition. DEATH: 1534 in Puri (some say drowned in the sea in a trance; others that he merged with the Jagannath deity).

questions.stem: SURDAS, the blind poet-saint, composed his devotional poetry primarily about which deity, and in which language?

options.option_text: BAAL KRISHNA (child Krishna) in BRAJ BHASHA — his magnum opus is the SUR SAGAR

questions.explanation: SURDAS (c. 1478-1583 — traditionally) — one of the eight poets of the ASHTACHHAP (founded by VALLABHACHARYA + his son Vitthalnath) at the Shrinathji temple of Govardhan (near Mathura). Devotee of BAAL KRISHNA — the child Krishna in his Vrindavan exploits. LANGUAGE: BRAJ BHASHA (a dialect of Hindi spoken around Mathura/Vrindavan). MAGNUM OPUS: SUR SAGAR ('Ocean of Sur') — 1,00,000 verses traditionally attributed (4,000-5,000 extant); focuses on Krishna's childhood pranks (gopikas' butter theft, Kaliya dance, lifting Govardhan, etc.) + Bhramar-Geet. BLINDNESS: Sur was said to be born blind; yet his poetry describes visual scenes (Krishna's face, Yamuna banks, gopis' expressions) so vividly that poets considered it divine vision; some scholars dispute whether he was literally blind. PHILOSOPHY: belonged to Vallabhacharya's PUSHTI MARGA (Shuddhadvaita / path of Divine Grace) sampradaya. Sur's bhajans are sung daily at Shrinathji Nathdwara (Rajasthan). ASHTACHHAP POETS: Surdas, Kumbhandas, Parmanandadas, Krishnadas (first four disciples of Vallabha) + Govindswami, Chaturbhujdas, Chhitswami, Nanddas (disciples of Vitthalnath). Surdas is celebrated alongside TULSIDAS (Rama) + KABIR (nirguna) + MEERA (Krishna-wife) as the SAGUNA + NIRGUNA twin pillars of N Indian bhakti.

questions.stem: Match the Bhakti saint with their region / language of composition: (1) TUKARAM — ? (2) NAMDEV — ? (3) BASAVA — ? (4) NARSINH MEHTA — ?
questions.explanation: BHAKTI SAINTS by REGION + LANGUAGE: (1) TUKARAM (1608-1650) — Maharashtra, MARATHI, devotee of Vithoba (Pandharpur); composed ABHANGAS; contemporary of Shivaji (guru-figure to him); drowned mysteriously at Dehu (disappeared 'taken to heaven by Vishnu', per tradition). (2) NAMDEV (1270-1350) — Maharashtra, MARATHI, also a Vithoba devotee; earlier saint of the Warkari tradition; 61 of his hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib. (3) BASAVA / BASAVANNA (1105-1168) — KARNATAKA, KANNADA; founded LINGAYATISM / VIRASHAIVISM; composed VACHANAS (free-verse sayings); fought caste + championed women's equality; built the Anubhava Mantapa (hall of spiritual experience) at Basavakalyan. (4) NARSINH MEHTA (1414-1481) — GUJARAT, GUJARATI; 'AADI KAVI' (first poet) of Gujarati; composed 'VAISHNAV JAN TO' — Gandhi's favourite bhajan (sung at Sabarmati + every 2 October to date). Devoted to Krishna. OTHER regional saints: (5) JNANESHWAR (1275-1296) — Marathi, wrote Jnaneshwari (Gita commentary); (6) EKNATH — Marathi; (7) ANDAL — Tamil (only female Alvar); (8) LAL DED (Lalleshwari) — Kashmiri, Shaivite; (9) SANKARDEV — Assamese (Ek-Sharana Naam-Dharma); (10) VEMANA — Telugu. Regional diversity of the Bhakti movement made it a pan-Indian phenomenon + enriched all vernaculars.

questions.stem: 'VAISHNAV JAN TO TENE KAHIYE' — Mahatma Gandhi's favourite bhajan describing the qualities of a true Vaishnavite — was composed by:

options.option_text: NARSINH MEHTA, the 15th-century Gujarati bhakti saint + 'Aadi Kavi' of Gujarati literature

questions.explanation: 'VAISHNAV JAN TO TENE KAHIYE, JE PEED PARAYI JANE RE' ('Call him a Vaishnav who feels the pain of others') — composed by NARSINH MEHTA (1414-1481), the Gujarati bhakti poet-saint of Junagadh. GANDHI'S FAVOURITE BHAJAN: sung every morning at Sabarmati Ashram + at Gandhi's memorial services at Rajghat each 2 October + 30 January. It distils Gandhi's own ethical vision — compassion, absence of ego, detachment, equal treatment of all, service to others. The lyrics list the qualities: (a) feels others' pain; (b) helps the needy without ego; (c) praises none, criticises none; (d) purifies the lineage of 71 generations; (e) faithful in word-thought-deed + worships Rama; (f) treats women as mother; (g) unmoved by greed or lust; (h) forsook false speech; (i) never touched others' wealth; (j) beyond illusions of Maya. NARSINH MEHTA: called the 'AADI KAVI' (first poet) of GUJARATI literature; devotee of KRISHNA; lived in Junagadh, Saurashtra; composed in Gujarati. Popular legends include: God himself filling in Narsinh's debts through miraculous hundis (promissory notes); Krishna dancing as Ras-Leela with him; giving him a HAAR (garland) from Krishna for an exchange of marriage at Dwarka. PM Modi has referenced 'Vaishnav Jan' often — reflects shared Gujarati heritage with Gandhi + Narsinh.
